## Research topics

### FacePrint: how faces become familiar people {#faceprint}

How does the brain turn an unfamiliar face into a person it knows, and does it treat a face generated by artificial intelligence the same way as a real one? FacePrint follows face identities from first sight to recognition. Participants view photographs of real people alongside AI-generated faces, learn some of these identities together with a voice and a short biography, and are later tested on recognition, including subtle morphs that blend one identity into another. Combining functional MRI and EEG, the project asks where and when the brain builds a representation of a specific person, and whether synthetic faces are learned, remembered, and judged like real ones.

### Natural and artificial intelligence in medicine

I focus on understanding both natural and artificial intelligence, and on using AI to improve diagnostics and therapeutics. A guiding conviction is that AI, applied responsibly, holds enormous potential for science and can accelerate discovery, particularly in healthcare. This topic connects my clinical and neuroscientific questions to modern machine-learning and generative-modelling methods.

To explore how the two kinds of intelligence shaped each other, visit **[The Intelligence Atlas](https://brain-machines-and-ideas-in-between.vercel.app/en)**, an interactive history of the ideas that travelled from biological cells to artificial systems and back again, told through connected discoveries, timelines, and demonstrations ([code](code-data.qmd#intelligence-atlas)).

### Neurophysiology of cognition and language perception

A central aim of my research line is to unravel the neurophysiological basis of cognition and of language perception in particular. Combining neuroimaging with electrophysiology, I study how neural activity supports perception and higher cognition, and how these processes are altered in brain pathologies. Characterising these mechanisms in both health and disease is a first step toward better diagnosis and treatment.

### Translational and functional neurosurgery

I am committed to transforming fundamental research insights into tangible clinical and neurosurgical solutions. My work spans functional neurosurgery, from deep brain stimulation and epilepsy surgery to electrocorticography (ECoG) and neuroprosthetics. Building on hands-on ECoG experience, I integrate principles from network neuroscience and artificial intelligence to pioneer therapeutic approaches that both deepen our understanding of brain mechanisms and enhance patient care.

## Methods

I answer these questions with neuroimaging, electrophysiology, machine learning, and computational modelling, and I develop the acquisition and analysis methods these questions demand, working across fundamental research and clinical settings.

### Neuroimaging

Neuroimaging, including ultra high-field MRI, maps where and how brain responses arise. I use it to relate neural activity to perception and cognition, and to characterise the changes that accompany brain pathologies.

### Method development and MRI sequence optimization

Answering these questions often demands better measurements than off-the-shelf tools provide. I develop new acquisition and analysis methods, with a particular emphasis on optimising ultra high-field 7 Tesla functional and anatomical MRI sequences, for both applied research and clinical applications. One example is the [MesoVeins project](https://mesoveins.com/), which maps the brain's mesoscopic veins, vessels too small for anatomical atlases yet large enough to resolve with MRI. Advancing what can be measured, and how reliably, feeds directly back into my questions about cognition, brain pathology, and neurosurgical care.

### Intracranial electrophysiology and ECoG

Recordings made directly from the cortex, including electrocorticography (ECoG) in patients undergoing epilepsy surgery, capture neural activity with high spatial and temporal precision. These recordings connect basic questions about cognition to the practical goals of functional neurosurgery and cortical mapping.

### Machine learning and neural decoding

Machine-learning and multivariate decoding methods ask what information a pattern of brain activity carries, rather than whether a region is simply more active. Applied to imaging and electrophysiology, they reveal how the brain represents perceptual and cognitive content.

### Generative AI {#generative-ai}

Generative models, including modern deep neural networks, offer both precise experimental control over the stimuli I study and a computational account of how the brain might represent them. Comparing human neural responses with the internal representations of these models tests which computational principles the brain actually uses, and links my cognitive-neuroscience work to my Neuro-AI program.

### Computational modeling {#computational-modeling}

Computational models turn a theory of brain function into equations that make testable predictions. Fitting these models to neural and behavioural data shows whether a proposed mechanism can actually produce what we observe, and provides a bridge from fundamental insight toward clinical application.

### Network neuroscience and complex systems

The brain is a network of interacting regions whose dynamics are often highly nonlinear. I draw on network neuroscience and ideas from complex-systems science, including chaos theory, to describe these dynamics and to relate them to function, dysfunction, and therapeutic intervention.
